---
title: "Student Lecture"
---

Once in the semester you are the one teaching. You take a topic this course does
not cover, spend twenty minutes making the class understand it, and **make the
room do something** while you are up there.

Twenty minutes is short, on purpose. It is long enough for one idea and one
activity, and too short for a survey. Pick a single question, answer it, and let
the room find the answer with you.

| | |
|---|---|
| Who | **You, alone.** |
| How long | **15 to 20 minutes**, once in the semester. |
| What it is worth | **10 points of your final grade.** See [how this course works](activities.md). |
| What is required | **An interactive part.** A talk with no activity does not count, however good the talk is. |
| How you claim one | Post the topic id on Discord in `#network-science`. One student per topic, first post wins. |
| Before you teach | Bring a one-page plan to office hours at least a week ahead. Your date is fixed when you claim the topic. |

## The one rule: the room has to do something

This is the part people get wrong, so it is worth being blunt about what counts.

**Counts.** A worksheet everyone fills in. A calculation the room does by hand on
a graph small enough to fit on paper. A prediction the room commits to before you
reveal the answer. Live coding where the class calls the shots. A physical
demonstration the class takes part in.

**Does not count.** "Any questions?" A poll whose result changes nothing that
follows. A demo the room only watches. A quiz at the end that tests whether they
were listening.

The test is simple: **if the class had not been there, would your twenty minutes
have gone differently?** If not, the activity is decoration.

::: {.callout-tip title="The activity is the hard half, not the easy half"}
Design it first and build the talk around it. Every topic below comes with a
suggested activity for exactly that reason: it is the part that decides whether
the lecture works, and it is the part people leave until the night before.

Whatever you design, do it yourself with a stopwatch first. An activity that
takes you four minutes takes the room ten.
:::

## Picking a topic

Every topic below is **adjacent to something you already know** and **not taught
in this course**. That is the whole design: you should be able to reach it with
what modules 1 to 9 gave you, and nobody in the room should have heard it from me
first.

"Start from" is a place to begin, not a reading list. One good paper plus the
textbook chapter around it is usually the right amount.

Twenty-six topics for a class of about thirteen, so nobody is left picking from
scraps.

## A. Networks this course never drew

Every network in this course had one kind of node, one kind of edge, no direction
of time and no sign. Each of these relaxes one of those.

**SL-01 · Bipartite networks and the projection trap**<br>
What happens to a network of actors and films when you throw the films away?<br>
*The room:* projects a five-actor, three-film table by hand and counts the triangles the projection invented. *Start from:* Newman, *Networks*, on bipartite networks.

**SL-02 · Temporal networks: paths that respect the clock**<br>
A path exists in the aggregated network. Can anything actually travel it?<br>
*The room:* gets a table of timestamped contacts and works out who could have infected whom, and who could not. *Start from:* Holme and Saramaki, "Temporal networks", Physics Reports 2012.

**SL-03 · Signed networks and structural balance**<br>
Is "the enemy of my enemy is my friend" a theorem or a folk saying?<br>
*The room:* signs the edges of a small graph, finds every unbalanced triangle, then repairs the graph with the fewest sign flips. *Start from:* Cartwright and Harary 1956; Leskovec, Huttenlocher and Kleinberg, "Signed networks in social media", CHI 2010.

**SL-04 · Beyond pairs: hypergraphs and simplicial complexes**<br>
Three people in a room is not three pairs. What does an edge list lose?<br>
*The room:* writes a list of three-author papers in both encodings, then finds a question only one of them can answer. *Start from:* Battiston et al., "Networks beyond pairwise interactions", Physics Reports 2020.

## B. Things that spread

Module 3 broke networks by removing nodes. These are about what moves across one
while it is still standing.

**SL-05 · The epidemic threshold**<br>
How infectious does a disease have to be before it takes off, and why does that depend on the hubs?<br>
*The room:* runs an SIR round by hand with dice on a ten-node graph, once on a lattice and once with a hub added. *Start from:* Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani, "Epidemic spreading in scale-free networks", PRL 2001.

**SL-06 · Complex contagion: when one exposure is not enough**<br>
Why do rumours travel on long ties and behaviours do not?<br>
*The room:* adopts under a two-neighbour rule on a ring lattice, then on the same lattice with shortcuts, and watches the shortcuts stop helping. *Start from:* Centola and Macy, "Complex contagions and the weakness of long ties", AJS 2007.

**SL-07 · Global cascades: the Watts threshold model**<br>
Why does one small shock do nothing and the next one, identical to it, take down everything?<br>
*The room:* each student is a node with a threshold on a card; run the cascade twice from two different seeds. *Start from:* Watts, "A simple model of global cascades on random networks", PNAS 2002.

**SL-08 · Opinion dynamics: the voter model**<br>
If everyone copies a random neighbour forever, what does the network end up believing?<br>
*The room:* coloured cards, one per student, five rounds of copy-a-neighbour; count how long consensus takes on a line against a clique. *Start from:* Castellano, Fortunato and Loreto, "Statistical physics of social dynamics", Reviews of Modern Physics 2009.

## C. Where structure comes from

Module 4 showed what degree distributions look like. These are about the
mechanisms that produce structure, and about testing whether a mechanism is
really there.

**SL-09 · Fitness: why the first mover does not always win**<br>
Preferential attachment says the oldest node wins. Google was not the first search engine.<br>
*The room:* grows two networks side by side on the board, one with fitness and one without, six steps each, and compares who ends up the hub. *Start from:* Bianconi and Barabasi, "Competition and multiscaling in evolving networks", EPL 2001.

**SL-10 · Network motifs**<br>
Which small subgraphs appear more often than chance, and what does that say about the system?<br>
*The room:* counts all three-node patterns in a small directed graph by hand, then in a rewired copy, and compares. *Start from:* Milo et al., "Network motifs: simple building blocks of complex networks", Science 2002.

**SL-11 · Exponential random graph models**<br>
How do you fit a *statistical* model to a network when you only have one of them?<br>
*The room:* proposes statistics for a small friendship graph, then argues about which set would be enough to reproduce it. *Start from:* Robins, Pattison, Kalish and Lusher, "An introduction to exponential random graph (p\*) models", Social Networks 2007.

**SL-12 · Synchronization: Kuramoto on a network**<br>
Fireflies, power grids and clapping audiences all lock into step. What structure makes that easy?<br>
*The room:* claps, first with everyone listening to everyone, then with each person listening to two neighbours only. Time both. *Start from:* Arenas, Diaz-Guilera, Kurths, Moreno and Zhou, "Synchronization in complex networks", Physics Reports 2008.

## D. Structure the community lens misses

Module 5 asked "which group is this node in?" Not every network is made of
groups, and these are what you ask instead.

**SL-13 · Core-periphery structure**<br>
What if a network has no communities at all, but a dense middle and a loose edge?<br>
*The room:* gets a shuffled adjacency matrix and reorders the rows by hand until the core is visible. *Start from:* Borgatti and Everett, "Models of core/periphery structures", Social Networks 2000.

**SL-14 · Node roles: within-module degree and participation**<br>
Two nodes have the same degree and sit in the same community. Are they doing the same job?<br>
*The room:* computes both coordinates for six labelled nodes and places each on the role diagram. *Start from:* Guimera and Amaral, "Functional cartography of complex metabolic networks", Nature 2005.

**SL-15 · How many communities? The detectability limit**<br>
Below a certain contrast no algorithm can find the communities. Not a hard problem: impossible.<br>
*The room:* splits two planted-partition graphs on paper, one above the threshold and one below, and finds out which was which. *Start from:* Decelle, Krzakala, Moore and Zdeborova, "Inference and phase transitions in the detection of modules in sparse networks", PRL 2011.

**SL-16 · Navigability: Kleinberg's exponent and greedy routing**<br>
Module 2 said short paths exist. Milgram's letters had to *find* them without a map. How?<br>
*The room:* routes a message across a printed grid with long-range shortcuts, forwarding greedily, and counts hops against its own guess. *Start from:* Kleinberg, "Navigation in a small world", Nature 2000.

## E. Learning and prediction on graphs

Modules 8 and 9 built embeddings and GNNs. These are the questions that arrive
the moment you try to use one.

**SL-17 · Link prediction without learning, and how to evaluate it honestly**<br>
Common neighbours is one line of code. When does it beat an embedding, and how would you know?<br>
*The room:* ranks candidate pairs by common neighbours for three hidden edges, then sees what a random split hid from it. *Start from:* Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg, "The link-prediction problem for social networks", JASIST 2007.

**SL-18 · Knowledge graphs and TransE**<br>
What changes when an edge has a *type*, and the type is part of what you embed?<br>
*The room:* does the vector arithmetic for three facts by hand and predicts a fourth. *Start from:* Bordes et al., "Translating embeddings for modeling multi-relational data", NeurIPS 2013.

**SL-19 · Over-squashing: the bottleneck deep GNNs cannot pass**<br>
Over-smoothing is not the only reason deep GNNs fail. What else breaks?<br>
*The room:* counts how many nodes get squeezed into one vector across a bridge, on a drawn graph, at two, three and four hops. *Start from:* Alon and Yahav, "On the bottleneck of graph neural networks and its practical implications", ICLR 2021.

**SL-20 · Explaining a GNN's prediction**<br>
The model says fraud. Which edges made it say so?<br>
*The room:* proposes the subgraph that explains a prediction, then checks it by deleting edges and re-running the aggregation by hand. *Start from:* Ying et al., "GNNExplainer: generating explanations for graph neural networks", NeurIPS 2019.

## F. Networks meet data and people

Where the network came from, and what it does once it is pointed at people.

**SL-21 · Networks built from correlations**<br>
Brain and gene networks are usually thresholded correlation matrices. What structure does that invent?<br>
*The room:* correlates four short series by hand, thresholds at two values, and watches the triangle count move. *Start from:* Zalesky, Fornito and Bullmore, "On the use of correlation as a measure of network connectivity", NeuroImage 2012.

**SL-22 · Weighted networks: which edges are real?**<br>
Every pair has some weight. How do you throw away the noise without throwing away the small nodes?<br>
*The room:* prunes one weighted graph twice, once with a global threshold and once locally, and compares what survives at a low-degree node. *Start from:* Serrano, Boguna and Vespignani, "Extracting the multiscale backbone of complex weighted networks", PNAS 2009.

**SL-23 · De-anonymizing a social graph**<br>
The names were removed. Why is that not anonymity?<br>
*The room:* gets an unlabelled graph plus one labelled fragment and re-identifies nodes from degree and neighbourhood alone. *Start from:* Narayanan and Shmatikov, "De-anonymizing social networks", IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2009.

**SL-24 · Ranking, recommendation and the glass ceiling**<br>
"People you may know" is a link predictor. What does running it for years do to a minority group?<br>
*The room:* runs three rounds of a recommend-the-most-connected rule on a small mixed graph and watches the shares diverge. *Start from:* Karimi, Genois, Wagner, Singer and Strohmaier, "Homophily influences ranking of minorities in social networks", Scientific Reports 2018.

**SL-25 · How false news spreads**<br>
True and false stories travel the same network. Why do they not travel the same way?<br>
*The room:* predicts which of six cascade shapes came from true stories, commits to an answer, and then sees it. *Start from:* Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, "The spread of true and false news online", Science 2018.

**SL-26 · Node-link or matrix: which picture answers which question**<br>
The hairball is not always the right drawing. When is a matrix better?<br>
*The room:* same network, two printouts; time it on "are these two nodes connected?" and on "find the densest group". *Start from:* Ghoniem, Fekete and Castagliola, "A comparison of the readability of graphs using node-link and matrix-based representations", InfoVis 2004.

## Propose your own

Bring one. It has to pass the two tests every topic above passes:

1. **It is not in this course.** Check the module pages first. PageRank, Louvain
   and over-smoothing are already taught, so a lecture on them is a review.
2. **You can name the activity in one sentence**, and it fits inside the twenty
   minutes along with the talk.

Propose it on Discord the way you would claim one from the list, and say what the
room will be doing.

## What a good one looks like

- **One question, stated in the first minute** and answered before the end.
  Twenty minutes will hold one idea properly or four badly.
- **The activity comes early**, not as an afterthought at the end. Let the room
  hit the difficulty *before* you resolve it. That is how every module here is
  built, and it is why the pen-and-paper exercise comes before the lecture
  rather than after it.
- **One worked example, small enough to see.** Six nodes on a slide beat a
  thousand-node hairball for anything you actually want to explain.
- **You say what you did not cover.** Naming the boundary of your twenty minutes
  is a sign that you know where it is.
